intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that vitelliform macular dystrophy-4 (VMD4) is caused by heterozygous, homozygous, or compound heterozygous mutation in the IMPG1 gene (602870) on chromosome 6q14.1.

paragraphs.text: Vitelliform macular dystrophies are inherited retinal dystrophies marked by yellow, round deposits seen on fundus examination. These deposits occur in juvenile Best macular dystrophy and in adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy. When Manes et al. (2013) reported IMPG1 mutations, the genetic cause was unknown in many affected individuals.

paragraphs.text: Meunier et al. (2014) described 11 patients from 3 families with IMPG1-related VMD. Families 1 and 2 had 10 affected members and showed autosomal dominant transmission. Family 3 had a sporadic case with presumed recessive transmission, with onset at age 38 years and a mean visual acuity of 20/50. Across the 13 patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations in their study, onset was late (mean 42 years) and visual impairment was moderate (mean visual acuity 20/40). Nine of the 13 patients had drusen-like lesions next to the vitelliform deposits, and EOG results were normal or borderline in 9 cases. On spectral-domain OCT, the vitelliform material lay above the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at all stages, between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines. The RPE was well preserved and of normal reflectivity. Meunier et al. (2014) noted that these features are not seen in classical BEST1 or PRPH2 vitelliform dystrophies.

paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) reported 2 simplex male patients with IMPG1 mutations. Patient 1, from a German family and aged 16 years at last report, had reduced visual acuity and central RPE abnormalities with foveal detachment in both eyes. He was the only affected member of his family. Patient 2, from a consanguineous Turkish family, was diagnosed with VMD at age 2 years. Over 8 years of follow-up he had fluctuating visual acuity of about 0.2 logMAR in both eyes. Color fundus images showed a single vitelliform lesion in the central macula of each eye but an otherwise normal fundus, with no satellite drusen. He also had a dome-shaped foveal detachment of the neurosensory retina with elongated photoreceptor outer segments and central circular hyperautofluorescence. At age 10 years, multifocal ERG was normal and the EOG Arden ratio was borderline to slightly low. Brandl et al. (2017) described the same sequence of stages in patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations. First came single central vitelliform lesions, with the material lying above a preserved Bruch membrane/RPE. The material was then resorbed, leaving an optically empty cavity, and finally there was central atrophy with RPE loss. Clinical symptoms tended to be more severe with IMPG1 mutations.

paragraphs.text: In a large family with autosomal dominant VMD, Manes et al. (2013) used gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.713T-G mutation in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution. They then found the same mutation in 2 other families with autosomal dominant VMD. They screened 144 probands with various forms of macular dystrophy and found 3 further IMPG1 mutations in 2 families with autosomal recessive VMD. Two affected individuals from one family were homozygous for a splice site mutation (c.807+1G-T). Two affected individuals from the other family were compound heterozygous for a leu154-to-pro (L154P) missense mutation and an arg507-to-ter (R507X) nonsense mutation. Manes et al. (2013) concluded that IMPG1 mutations cause both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive VMD, and suggested that impairment of the interphotoreceptor matrix might be a general cause of VMD.

paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) screened IMPG1 and IMPG2 in 106 VMD patients who had tested negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations. They found IMPG1 mutations in 2 simplex cases with onset in early childhood. A German patient carried a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution. Brandl et al. (2017) noted that this was the second missense mutation affecting IMPG1 residue Leu238 in a VMD patient, after L238R. A patient from a consanguineous Turkish family was homozygous for a c.807+5G-A splice site mutation, and segregation analysis showed that both parents were heterozygous. In a minigene assay in HEK293 cells, this mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of the transcripts, and the authors suggested that the aberrant mRNA likely undergoes nonsense-mediated decay. The heterozygous parents were asymptomatic and had normal retinal imaging. Brandl et al. (2017) suggested that the correctly spliced transcripts provide enough functional IMPG1 to prevent even subclinical abnormalities in heterozygous carriers. They proposed that defective IMPG1 causes disease through an as yet unknown dominant-negative effect or through haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Gupta et al. (2021) found a heterozygous L154P mutation in the IMPG1 gene in a 25-year-old woman with early-onset vitelliform dystrophy. They suggested that this mutation, which has been implicated in adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy, may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state, and noted that further studies were needed.

checks.claim: Gupta et al. (2021) found a heterozygous L154P mutation in the IMPG1 gene in a 25-year-old woman with early-onset vitelliform dystrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: UNUSUAL EARLY-ONSET VITELLIFORM DYSTROPHY POSSIBLY LINKED TO THE INTERPHOTORECEPTOR MATRIX PROTEOGLYCAN-1 P.LEU154PRO MUTATION.
checks.explanation: The title calls the condition early-onset vitelliform dystrophy, and the results say genetic testing found a heterozygous p.Leu154Pro mutation in IMPG1 in the 25-year-old patient. The title frames the link as 'possibly' causal.

checks.claim: The IMPG1 L154P mutation has been implicated in adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: heterozygous for the p.Leu154Pro interphotoreceptor matrix proteoglycan-1 (IMPG1) mutation implicated in adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that this mutation has been implicated in adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy.

checks.claim: Gupta et al. (2021) suggested that the IMPG1 L154P mutation may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state, and noted that further studies were needed.
checks.evidence_quote: The p.Leu154Pro IMPG1 mutation may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state. Further studies are necessary.
checks.explanation: The claim restates the abstract's conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Olivier et al. (2021) used exome sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant RP and identified a splice variant in IMPG1. They then found the same variant in individuals from 2 families with either RP or VMD. A retrospective study of patients with RP or VMD found 8 more families with different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1. In all, they screened 596 families with RP or VMD by gene panel testing and exome sequencing. They concluded that monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants are associated with RP, similar to what has been reported for IMPG2.

checks.claim: Olivier et al. (2021) used exome sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa and identified a splice variant in IMPG1.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome sequencing was carried out for identifying the disease-causing gene in a family with autosomal dominant RP.
checks.explanation: The Results section adds: 'Exome sequencing of a family with RP revealed a splice variant in IMPG1.'

checks.claim: Olivier et al. (2021) found the same IMPG1 splice variant in individuals from 2 families with either retinitis pigmentosa or vitelliform macular dystrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: Subsequently, the same variant was identified in individuals from two families with either RP or VMD.

checks.claim: A retrospective study by Olivier et al. (2021) of patients with retinitis pigmentosa or vitelliform macular dystrophy found 8 more families with different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1.
checks.evidence_quote: A retrospective study of patients with RP or VMD revealed eight additional families with different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1.

checks.claim: Olivier et al. (2021) screened a total of 596 families with retinitis pigmentosa or vitelliform macular dystrophy by gene panel testing and exome sequencing.
checks.evidence_quote: Gene panel testing and exome sequencing were performed in 596 RP and VMD families to identified additional IMPG1 variants.
checks.explanation: The family count (596) and both methods match the abstract.

checks.claim: Olivier et al. (2021) concluded that monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants are associated with retinitis pigmentosa, similar to what has been reported for IMPG2.
checks.evidence_quote: This study discusses a previously unreported association between monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants and RP. Notably, similar observations have been reported for IMPG2.
checks.explanation: The draft restates the abstract's conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2013) noted that IMPG1 encodes SPACR, a component of the extracellular matrix domains of rod and cone photoreceptors. Structural modeling indicated that the L238R substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR.

checks.claim: IMPG1 encodes SPACR, a component of the extracellular matrix domains of rod and cone photoreceptors.
checks.evidence_quote: IMPG1 encodes the SPACR protein, a component of the rod and cone photoreceptor extracellular matrix domains.

checks.claim: Structural modeling by Manes et al. (2013) indicated that the IMPG1 L238R substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR.
checks.evidence_quote: Structural modeling indicates that the p.Leu238Arg substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of SPACR.

paragraphs.text: Meunier et al. (2014) recommended screening IMPG1 and IMPG2 in patients with adult-onset vitelliform dystrophy who have moderate visual impairment, drusen-like lesions, normal RPE reflectivity on spectral-domain OCT, and vitelliform deposits between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines.

checks.claim: Meunier et al. (2014) recommended screening IMPG1 and IMPG2 in patients with adult-onset vitelliform dystrophy who have moderate visual impairment, drusen-like lesions, normal retinal pigment epithelium reflectivity on spectral-domain OCT, and vitelliform deposits between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines.
checks.evidence_quote: These genes should be screened in adult-onset vitelliform dystrophy with (1) moderate visual impairment, (2) drusen-like lesions, (3) normal reflectivity of the RPE line on SD-OCT, and (4) vitelliform deposits located between ellipsoid and interdigitation lines on SD-OCT.
checks.explanation: The claim restates the abstract's screening recommendation.

paragraphs.text: Meunier et al. (2014) screened 49 families with VMD who were negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations. IMPG1 or IMPG2 was causal in 8% (4 families: 3 with IMPG1 and 1 with IMPG2 mutations).

checks.claim: Meunier et al. (2014) screened 49 families with vitelliform macular dystrophy who were negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations.

checks.claim: Among 49 BEST1/PRPH2-negative vitelliform macular dystrophy families screened by Meunier et al. (2014), IMPG1 or IMPG2 was causal in 8% (4 families).
checks.evidence_quote: IMPG1 and IMPG2 are new causal genes in 8% of families negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations.
checks.explanation: The 8% figure is stated, and 4 of 49 families is about 8%.

checks.claim: Among the 4 families with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations identified by Meunier et al. (2014), 3 had IMPG1 mutations and 1 had an IMPG2 mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: IMPG1 was the causal gene in 3 families (IMPG1 1-3, 11 patients) and IMPG2 in a fourth family (2 patients).
checks.explanation: Three IMPG1 families and one IMPG2 family are stated.

paragraphs.text: Olivier et al. (2021) used morpholinos to knock down Impg1 and its paralog Impg2 in medaka fish. The resulting phenotype matched that seen in the families and included shorter rod and cone photoreceptor outer segments.

paragraphs.text: In a large family with autosomal dominant vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD4), Manes et al. (2013) used gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.713T-G transversion in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution. They then found the mutation in 2 other families with autosomal dominant VMD and the same phenotype. Structural modeling indicated that the substitution destabilizes the conserved SEA1 domain of the SPACR protein.

checks.claim: Manes et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.713T-G transversion in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution, in a large family with autosomal dominant VMD4.
checks.evidence_quote: In a large family with autosomal-dominant VMD, gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing led to the identification of a c.713T>G (p.Leu238Arg) IMPG1 mutation
checks.explanation: T>G is a transversion; heterozygosity is implied by the dominant inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Gupta et al. (2021) identified a heterozygous L154P mutation in the IMPG1 gene in a 25-year-old woman with a symptomatic scotoma, decreased vision, small yellow foveal spots in both eyes, and disruption of the foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones on OCT. They suggested that the mutation may cause symptomatic outer retinal disturbance in the heterozygous state, and noted that further studies were needed.

paragraphs.text: In a 16-year-old German boy with VMD4, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7 of the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution. He had reduced visual acuity and central RPE abnormalities with foveal detachment in both eyes, and he was the only affected member of his family. Brandl et al. (2017) noted that this was the second missense mutation affecting residue Leu238 in a VMD patient, after L238R.

checks.evidence_quote: Thus, the current finding of a second missense mutation affecting amino acid p.(Leu238) in a patient with VMD supports the causative role of defective IMPG1 molecules

paragraphs.text: In a boy from a consanguineous Turkish family who was diagnosed with VMD4 at age 2 years, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a homozygous c.807+5G-A splice site mutation in the IMPG1 gene. Segregation analysis showed that both parents were heterozygous. The parents were asymptomatic and had normal retinal imaging. In a minigene assay in HEK293 cells, the mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of the transcripts.
